description: Headings, paragraphs, links, and images — the four elements behind almost every page.

screens.body:
Headings run from <h1> (biggest, most important) down to <h6> (smallest). They're not about size, though — they're about STRUCTURE.

Use one <h1> per page: the page's main topic. Then <h2> for sections, <h3> for sub-sections, and so on — like an outline.

Never pick a heading level for its look. Style with CSS; choose headings by meaning.

options: One h1 for the page topic, then h2/h3 for sections
As many h1s as look good
Always h6, styled bigger with CSS

screens.body:
Links are made with <a> (short for "anchor"). The href attribute holds the destination: a page, a site, or an email.

The text between the tags is what visitors click. "Click here" is lazy — link text should say where it goes: "See pricing".

Links can point anywhere: another page (/about), another site (https://…), or even a spot on the same page (#menu).

check.question: Which makes a working link to /about?

code.snippet: See pricing MO-WEBCO Jump to the menu

screens.heading: Links: the web's superpower
screens.keyPoint: text. href = destination; the text should say where it goes.

screens.body: Images use . It needs two attributes: src (where the picture file is) and alt (a text description of the picture). never wraps content, so it has no closing tag — it's self-closing: . Browsers show a broken-image icon if src is wrong, so double-check the file path. Keep images near your HTML file or in a tidy folder like /images.
screens.heading: Images
screens.keyPoint: needs src (file) and alt (description). No closing tag.

screens.body:
Alt text is read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. So write it like you're describing the picture to a friend on the phone.

Good: alt="A calico cat napping in a sunbeam". Bad: alt="image" or alt="cat.jpg" — those say nothing useful.

If an image is pure decoration (a background swirl), an empty alt="" tells screen readers to skip it. That's the one time empty is correct.

options: alt="A calico cat napping in a sunbeam"
check.question: Which alt text is best?

screens.heading: Alt text: describing pictures
screens.keyPoint: Alt text describes the image for people who can't see it. Be specific.

screens.body:
Need bold or italic? You have two pairs. <b> and <i> just change the look: bold and italic, no extra meaning.

<strong> and <em> (emphasis) ALSO change the look — but they add meaning. Screen readers stress <strong> and <em> when reading aloud.

Rule of thumb: important warning or key term → <strong>; a word you'd stress while speaking → <em>. Pure styling → CSS instead.

options: <strong> — it marks the text as important
check.question: For a "Do not share your password" warning, which is better?

code.snippet:

screens.heading: Emphasis: b/i vs strong/em
screens.keyPoint: <strong> and <em> carry meaning; <b> and <i> are just looks.

Two tiny self-closing tags round out text basics.
